book: 020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings

chapters.relation: The editor's introduction stages poker and philosophy as twin crafts of risk: 'philosopher' was once slang for a card cheat, Socrates and Wild Bill Hickok both died for keeping villainous company, and the Buddha's six years to enlightenment are measured against the Birdcage Theater's eight-year poker game. It recruits Nietzsche's 'live dangerously' and Kierkegaard's leap of faith to defend the all-in as the only meaningful way to live, then traces probability from Cardano's Book on Games of Chance to Pascal's wager that believing in God is the smarter bet — the ancestor of today's pot-odds reasoning. Chris Ferguson's PhD, Annie Duke's psycholinguistics, and Jesse May's 'the trick to poker is mastering the luck — that's philosophy' set up the book's Texas Hold'em focus.

Ventimiglia mines No-Limit Hold'em for seven lessons philosophers also teach: we lack certain knowledge (Descartes' cogito is the famous quest for certainty, but philosophy's own history of disagreement proves uncertainty is the human condition), and like William James against Clifford we must still believe and act without the nuts — waiting for pocket aces while the blinds eat you alive is no strategy. Risking everything echoes Thoreau's escape from lives of quiet desperation, trusting hunches over arithmetic follows Thoreau and Peirce's sentimentalism, and the Darwin-and-Spencer competition of tournament poker hides a deeper cooperative social contract: get caught cheating and you are out of the game. It closes with Plato's four classic virtues from the Republic — wisdom, courage, moderation, and the justice of a balanced soul — as the perfection of a poker player.

Belliotti tells of busting 'Pickle Puss' with flopped queens and of tight 'Howard the Vest' paying off his flopped full house to ask whether Marx's diagnoses — alienation in four forms, exploitation of surplus value, and false consciousness spread through the ideological superstructure by the economic base — condemn poker. He argues no: unlike coerced factory labor, poker is freely chosen creative activity that energizes our species-being like an absorbed artist, as Doyle 'Texas Dolly' Brunson's road-gambler career and his famous ten-deuce full-house call against Jessie Alto at the 1976 WSOP (and the 1980 loss to Stu Ungar's gutshot) show. Poker may still launder capitalist ideology — antes that lure investment, zero-sum rivalry, rugged individualism — but the owner-worker exploitation Marx feared has no equivalent at an equal-buy-in table.

Young reads David Sklansky's fundamental theorem of poker — play as if you could see all the cards — through Aristotle and Husserl. Aristotle's phronesis and virtue-as-habituation explain how excellent players come to perceive the particulars (pot odds, opponent tendencies, the best possible hand) and stay unharmed even when losing with the best play, while Husserl's Cartesian Meditations, translated hand-by-hand into poker terms, supply analogical appresentation for knowing the other minds seated across the table. Chris Moneymaker's 2003 'Bluff of the Century' all-in with nothing against Sammy Farha shows how bluffing randomizes play and lets you shape the truth you seek, until a slow-played quad aces ends the night in Socratic humility about the limits of knowledge.

Sanders splits poker into two philosophical styles. The Rationalist — Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason, Pascal's domestication of chance into probability — plays like Sklansky, Chris Ferguson, and Howard Lederer, whose temptation is the paralysis of analysis; the Existentialist — Sartre's existence precedes essence, Camus' scorn for the absurd, Kierkegaard's leap of faith taken without decisive evidence — plays like Gus Hansen calling Antonio Esfandiari's $334,000 all-in re-raise with ten-high. A Russell-and-Popper-style regress of predictions (knowing a prediction changes its outcome) becomes the tournament 'hall of mirrors' of intentions read in Phil Ivey and Johnny Chan, and the chapter lands on Richard Taylor's existentialist point that meaning comes from committed doing, at the table as in life.

Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.

Ellis analyzes expert poker as thought attribution, spelling the iterations out to the sixth order in a Big Slick hand against T.J. Cloutier, then argues via Quine's 'gavagai' rabbit and Davidson's interpretationism that attributing thoughts to opponents requires assuming deep shared belief — which explains why pros misread novices whose minds they cannot model. The centerpiece is Dan Harrington's reconstruction of Daniel Negreanu's 2004 river raise against Freddy Deeb as a set of fourth-order-or-below attributions (Deeb will read a small raise as a lure bet and fold the best hand), not one towering thought. It ends asking how anyone ever learns what an opponent thinks from actions that are a vector of beliefs and desires, and notes poker forces rare deep agreement among strangers worldwide.

Bassham and Marchese catalogue seven critical-thinking traps that cost even good players money: self-serving bias (Rochester Ricky donating $10,000 to Brunson's Texas road gamblers), short-term thinking (aimed at Aristippus' live-for-today hedonism), the availability heuristic (Brunson's red eights on a four-flush board), the fundamental attribution error (crediting wins to skill and losses to luck), loss aversion (which breeds tight-passive 'rocks'), superstitious thinking (Alexander ripping the pockets off his shirt for luck), and the gambler's fallacy (Ken Warren's bogus 'rush' theory of streaky cards). The moral is psychological self-knowledge: great players must know their own cognitive frailties, because — as Clint Eastwood says — a man's got to know his limitations.

Fallis asks which probability should guide a poker decision, working one Big Slick hand ($20,000 call into a $160,000 pot) through four candidates: objective chances (already 100% or 0% under the dealt river card — useless without cheating), the TV viewer's WPT-cam probability, Sklansky's Fundamental-Theorem probability given the opponent's exact cards, and Beebee and Papineau's relative probability given what you actually know (9.5%, under the 11.1% pot-odds threshold, so fold). David Lewis's Principal Principle frames the first option, and Jack Good's value-of-information theorem explains why Sklansky's ideal remains worth approximating: additional information can never hurt your expectation.

Northcott loses his first casino tournament to a fluky inside straight and mines the bad beat for philosophy of science: objective odds collapse into knowledge-relative probabilities (a card-tracking magician would assign different numbers to the very same draw), Laplacean determinism versus quantum chance bears on whether decision theory presupposes free will, and bad-beat counterfactuals — 'I'd have won the tournament but for that hand' — get David Lewis's possible-worlds closeness analysis and Hume's counterfactual account of causation, with no settled verdict. Even game theory cannot deliver a perfect system: a Nash-equilibrium strategy is only optimal against other optimal players, so the mindless all-in 'Stupidus' beats it. Conclusion: no can't-lose system exists, and poker will never be a game for robots.

Lucey opens with the ultimate bad beat — four aces losing a $180,000 jackpot share to two straight flushes — to ask what poker knowledge could have told you, and answers with Ryle's distinction between 'knowing that' and 'knowing how' from The Concept of Mind. Knowing-that is a priori and internalized: hand rankings and five conditionals for spotting the best possible hand (board pairs, three flush cards, three-to-a-straight spans, diamond threats). Knowing-how is dispositional — folding 2-9 'Montana bananas' despite the rare flopped full house, adjusting value between limit and no-limit — and with Israel Scheffler's vertical spectrum from competence to mastery it explains why poker skill is endlessly refinable, which is why the game is so addictive and so frustrating.

Huss tests four models of bluffing on one K-9 all-in: it is not lying, because everyone at the table expects deception, so the victim is never Frankfurt's 'twice deceived' (and Kant's argument that lying fails where everyone lies applies); it is not bullshit, because Frankfurt's bullshitter ignores the facts a poker player cannot afford to ignore; it is not pure acceptance in Jonathan Cohen's sense, since bluffing adds deception to acting-as-if; and it is not full self-deception, since nobody can make themselves believe that 2+2=5 or that 4-7 offsuit is pocket aces. Good bluffing is an art blending all four: deceiving about hand and beliefs, prying attention away from your cards, acting as if, and trying — and necessarily failing — to fool yourself.

Barnhill and Solomon use Robert Varkonyi's staged five-minute 'agony' over pocket aces — pure theater that lured Ralph Perry into an all-in at the 2002 WSOP (and later busted Phil Hellmuth's A-K with Q-10 suited) — to ask when poker deception is morally acceptable and when it crosses the line: the towed-car lie, the fake-Marine claim, racist goading, and collusion are wrong. Their answer is an implicit-permission theory: by sitting down, players waive the right not to be deceived, but only where deception tests poker skills, so bluffs, disguised strength, and silently reading exposed cards are fine. The underlying order of the implicit rules — the game must test only poker skills — also explains everyday white lies and what you may tell a mugger.

Koepsell applies Searle's method from The Construction of Social Reality — picture the game, subtract an attribute, ask whether what remains still counts — to decide whether online poker is really poker. After tracing poker's lineage from Brag and primero through the 1830s draw to Texas Hold'em's communal cards, he argues poker's essence includes the artful, theatrical bluff carried by physical tells, mystique, and etiquette, so the disembodied online game, where only bets and chat remain, is 'a subset of the game' lacking the social institution that makes poker poker. His father's farm-purchase negotiation shows the same non-liar's bluff at work off the felt.

Hahn reads Doyle Brunson's Super System — 'I go into a Poker game with the idea of completely destroying it' — as applied Machiavelli: The Prince's fox and lion become the bluffer and the bully chip leader, 'better to be feared than loved' justifies cutting even old friend Sailor Roberts's throat at the table, and swift decisive attack (Tex Barch stomped out of the 2005 WSOP) avoids sowing the seeds of vengeance. Fortune rules half our events — the river card that fills an opponent's inside straight — so virtù means building dikes against the flood, as Cesare Borgia failed to do when his papal patron died. Sun Tzu's 'when able, seem to be unable' supplies the same disguise of strength in poker and in war.

Hamilton, unsettled that his seventeen-year-old daughter Tess has taken up poker, sorts the game's motives three ways. Competition is morally justified as a mutual quest for excellence with respect for worthy opponents (Robert Simon; Phil Hellmuth's tilt as the counterexample to Brunson's class); fellowship is Aristotle's three friendships — utility, pleasure, and the virtue friendship that shapes character — enacted in his father's VFW games and in Louise and Sailor Roberts keeping vigil when Brunson had four months to live, with Kant's rare moral friendship and C.S. Lewis's side-by-side companionship filling it out; but profit-playing invites the three-phase slide into pathological gambling addiction. His verdict: the motive decides the morality — poker is justified for competition and friendship, not for profit.

Lindholm retells Stu Ungar's 1981 WSOP repeat — the 'Jews' (Ungar, Perry Green, Jay Heimowitz) against the 'Texans' (Ken Smith, Gene Fisher, Bill Smith) — through Levinas's Talmudic lecture 'The Temptation of Temptation.' Philosophy's sin is wanting to know before doing, while the Jews at Sinai accepted the Torah before knowing what it contained; the gambler's decision under risk, like Ungar's triple all-ins and final A-Q call against Green, enacts the same ethical priority of doing over knowing, so to lose is still to win if you dared to decide. Ethics as first philosophy — responsibility to the Other prior to comprehension, born of Levinas's Holocaust losses — closes the loop: unlike poker, life is not zero-sum, and deciding to decide lets everyone win.

Stoehr finds Hobbes in the saloon: poker in classic Westerns — Hatfield's farewell game in Stagecoach, and the cheating scene where Wyatt Earp first crosses Doc Holliday in My Darling Clementine — dramatizes the tension between the lawless state of nature ('solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short') and the rule-governed community built by an implicit social contract, with caught cheaters (Chihuahua signaling hole cards) marking where play reverts to primal vengeance. Poker itself is a Hobbesian paradox: a communal social event built on winner-takes-all competition, exercising both logic and intuition within luck's hard limits. The morally ambiguous Fordian hero — Doc Holliday above all — lives at the same crossroads of civilization and wilderness as the card table.

Housel surveys a century of poker on screen — from the Tombstone Birdcage Theater's 'bird in a gilded cage' through Maverick, The Gambler, Rounders, and ESPN's Tilt with its brothel-break 'Matador' — to show women cast as eye-candy, damsels, or flukes (Joanne Woodward winning a high-stakes game without knowing how to play). Against the myth stands Annie Duke, who beat her brother Howard on the way to the 2004 Tournament of Champions title. The argument: poker rewards reading and projecting emotion, so women socialized into emotional intelligence hold an edge over macho men who suppress it — a retooled Stoicism fusing Epictetus's 'make the best use of what is in your power' with Gilligan's care ethics, backed by Nietzsche's trust in the senses and Sun Tzu's 'pretend inferiority and encourage his arrogance.'

Hamblet, a violence scholar, asks why the 'cheating game' fascinates us, weighing Charles Lamb's Mrs. Battle (cards as dream-fighting that harmlessly dissipates aggression) and Georges Bataille's 'unproductive expenditure' before concluding that no-limit hold'em amplifies rather than vents hostility. Poker's history is soaked in blood — Mississippi riverboats, Bugsy Siegel's Las Vegas, and twice-indicted killer Benny Binion founding the WSOP from his Horseshoe ('I never killed anyone who didn't deserve it') — because a game whose core skills are lying and aggression attracts and rewards criminals. Lou Krieger's claim that poker mirrors capitalism and democracy is tested against David Callahan's cheating culture: Martha Stewart condoned because everybody does it, and the model poker-playing politician was Nixon.

holes.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
holes.what: Russian novelist whose Notes from Underground and The Gambler are standardly treated as the overture to existentialism, defending the irrational, risk-embracing life against rational self-interest.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is built entirely on his two novellas and his roulette addiction, using them to argue that gambling is an existential activity beyond reason.

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: American philosopher of language and mind whose interpretationism holds that attributing meanings, beliefs and thoughts to others requires assuming they share most of our beliefs (charity), with action a 'vector' of belief and desire.
holes.why: Chapter 17 applies Davidson's shared-belief thesis and vector model to explain how poker players attribute third- and fourth-order thoughts to opponents and why pros misread novices.

holes.name: The Principle of Charity (shared belief in interpretation)
holes.what: Davidson's demand that interpretation proceed by maximizing agreement, since identifying disagreement presupposes a background of largely shared true beliefs.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses it to show why Negreanu's bluff against Deeb needs a web of shared assumptions and why poker at its best forces deep agreement among strangers.

holes.name: Lewis's Principal Principle (chance as a guide to credence)
holes.what: David Lewis's norm that rational credence should defer to objective chance, challenged by Beebee and Papineau's relative probabilities computed only from what the agent knows.
holes.why: Chapter 19 evaluates four candidate probabilities for poker decisions against Lewis's principle and concludes only Beebee-Papineau relative probability is a usable guide at the table.

holes.name: Knowing How vs Knowing That
holes.what: Ryle's distinction from The Concept of Mind between propositional knowledge (knowing that) and skill as intelligent disposition (knowing how).
holes.why: Chapter 21 organizes all poker knowledge into these two Rylean categories, from internalized hand rankings to the dispositions that make a player fold bad hands.

holes.name: Belief versus Acceptance
holes.what: Jonathan Cohen's distinction between involuntary belief (a feeling that something is true) and the voluntary policy of accepting a proposition — acting as if it were true for practical purposes.
holes.why: Chapter 23 tests bluffing-as-acceptance against bluffing-as-lying and bluffing-as-bullshit, concluding good bluffing partly consists in acting as if one held a stronger hand.

holes.name: The Construction of Social Reality (institutional facts)
holes.what: Searle's account of how collective intentionality creates institutional facts — X counts as Y in context C — so games, money and law exist only by collective recognition.
holes.why: Chapter 25 uses Searle's social-objects method to define poker's necessary features and argue that online poker lacks the social institution that makes poker poker.
